maths_errors.text: Multiplying by a scalar k scales both components by k — this changes the magnitude but keeps the direction (or reverses it if k is negative).
maths_errors.correction: Multiplying by k multiplies the length by |k|. The length does not change when k = 1 or k = −1, and when k = 0 the result is the zero vector, which has no direction. The statement should say: 'the length is multiplied by |k|; the direction stays the same if k > 0 and is reversed if k < 0.'

missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never links column vectors to translating a shape. Nothing asks the student to describe a translation (object to image) with a column vector, or to apply one to a shape.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: diagrammatic and column representations of vectors
missing_spec_content.why: Only column representation is used. Drawing a vector on a grid, reading a column vector from a drawn arrow, and showing a + b or ka as arrows on a diagram are not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: use vectors to construct geometric arguments and proofs
missing_spec_content.why: Parallel lines, midpoints and collinearity are only named (formula whenToUse, keyFacts[2]). The lesson does not teach how to write a vector path in terms of a and b, use ratios or midpoints on a line segment, or set out a proof.

above_gcse.why: AQA 8300 G24/G25 do not require the magnitude notation |a|. It sits among the five required operations as if it were core content, which could mislead the student about what is examined. (Pythagoras on a grid is assessed separately under G20.)

cases_not_modelled.case: diagrammatic vectors on a grid (drawing or reading a vector arrow)

cases_not_modelled.case: multiplication by a negative or fractional scalar

cases_not_modelled.why: Mentioned in slides[1].whenToUse ('finding midpoints using vectors') but never modelled.

density.text: The same column vector applied to different starting points creates parallel, equal-length movements — so two vectors are equal if and only if they have the same column vector, regardless of where they start.
density.why: One sentence carries three ideas: position-independence, parallel and equal length, and the condition for equality. It also uses 'if and only if' with no explanation.

density.text: Column vector: (x over y) where x = horizontal shift (+ right, − left), y = vertical shift (+ up, − down)  |  Addition: a + b = (a₁ + b₁) over (a₂ + b₂)  |  Subtraction: a − b = (a₁ − b₁) over (a₂ − b₂)  |  Scalar multiplication: k·a = (ka₁) over (ka₂)  |  Magnitude: |a| = √(x² + y²)
density.why: Five separate rules are packed into one line, separated by bars. The subscripts a₁, a₂ and the word 'over' (meaning stacked in a column) are used without being explained.

density.text: Reversing the sign when finding −a or when subtracting — forgetting that −(−1) = +1 when subtracting a negative component.
density.why: Read literally, the first clause names the correct method (reversing the sign to find −a) as the mistake. The real error, mishandling a double negative, only appears after the dash, so a first-time reader may be confused about what to avoid.

density.text: Three points are collinear if the vector between any two of them is a scalar multiple of the vector between another two.
density.why: This is abstract with no example, for instance 'if AC = 3AB, then A, B, C are collinear because the vectors are parallel and share point A'.
